steps.q: Where does cavitation start in a centrifugal pump?
steps.title: Pressure walk
steps.summary: Cavitation starts at the impeller eye, the lowest-pressure point in the pump. Pressure falls along the suction pipe, dips further where the liquid speeds up into the eye, and rises again as the impeller throws it out to the discharge.

steps.q: Bubbles form when the pressure at the eye falls below...
steps.title: Why bubbles?
steps.summary: A liquid boils when the pressure on it falls below its vapour pressure, whatever its temperature. Water boils at about 70 °C on Everest; at the impeller eye the pressure can fall low enough for liquid to boil at room temperature. Hot liquids and volatile solvents, with higher vapour pressures, cavitate first.

opts.t: The vapour pressure of the liquid

steps.q: What happens to the bubbles when they reach the high-pressure part of the impeller?
steps.title: Bubble → POP
steps.summary: Vapour bubbles formed at the eye are carried into higher pressure and collapse. Each collapse fires a micro-jet of liquid at the vane, thousands of times a second, pitting the metal. Signs: a gravel-like noise, vibration, falling head and pitted vanes at overhaul.

opts.t: They leave as gas at the discharge

steps.q: Which change gives the pump more NPSH available?
steps.title: NPSH = savings account
steps.summary: NPSH available works like a savings account. Deposits: the pressure on the liquid surface and the liquid height above the pump. Withdrawals: the vapour pressure and suction friction. The balance must beat the pump's NPSHr plus a margin, so raise the level, keep the liquid cool and keep the suction short, wide and clean.

opts.t: A higher liquid level in the tank

steps.q: A column bottoms pump handles liquid at its boiling point. What is its NPSH available?
steps.title: Boiling liquid
steps.summary: For liquid at its boiling point, the vessel pressure equals the vapour pressure, so the two cancel. NPSH available is only the liquid height above the pump minus the suction friction, which is why bottoms pumps sit several metres below the column with short, wide suction lines.

opts.t: Liquid height above the pump, minus friction

steps.q: A pump starts crackling and its discharge pressure swings. What do you check first?
steps.title: Pump crackling?
steps.summary: Check the suction side first: a clogged strainer, a low tank level or a hotter liquid all reduce NPSH available. Never throttle the suction valve; control flow on the discharge side. If the pump runs far out on its curve, closing the discharge a little cuts flow, friction and NPSHr.

opts.t: Strainer, tank level and liquid temperature

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Pumps are my enemy, and I'm theirs. Six questions on NPSH and cavitation. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now try your own pump in the NPSH calculator.

outro-reel.text: Try your own pump in the free NPSH calculator, on pharmacheme dot in.

q1.text: Question 1. Where does cavitation start in a centrifugal pump?

q1-r0.text: The discharge?! That's the highest pressure in the whole pump. Bubbles would never survive there.

q1-r1.text: Look at you! Yes, the impeller eye.

q1-r2.text: The seal?! It leaks and complains, sure. But it doesn't make bubbles.

q1-r3.text: The delivery tank?! The liquid has already left the building.

q1-ans.text: The answer: at the impeller eye.

q1-b0.text: Follow the pressure from the tank into the pump.

q1-b1.text: In the suction pipe, friction eats a little of it.

q1-b2.text: Then it squeezes into the impeller eye and speeds up. Faster liquid, lower pressure. This is the lowest point.

q1-b3.text: The impeller then flings it out and the pressure climbs. The discharge is the high pressure end.

q1-b4.text: Like a crowd at a metro gate: the squeeze happens right at the gate, not on the platform.

q2.text: Question 2. Bubbles form when the pressure at the eye falls below...

q2-r0.text: Atmospheric?! Then every pump on a vacuum receiver would fizz all day long.

q2-r1.text: Exactly. The vapour pressure. You're on fire. Not literally, please.

q2-r2.text: Zero gauge?! That's just atmospheric pressure wearing a disguise.

q2-r3.text: NPSHr is what the pump demands. It's not a pressure the liquid boils at. Nice try, though.

q2-ans.text: The answer: the vapour pressure of the liquid.

q2-b0.text: Every liquid has a vapour pressure. Drop the pressure below it, and the liquid boils, even when it's cold.

q2-b1.text: On Everest, water boils at about seventy degrees, because the air pressure is so low.

q2-b2.text: Your impeller eye is a tiny Everest. Drop the pressure there below the vapour pressure, and the liquid boils at room temperature.

q2-b3.text: Hot liquids and volatile solvents have a high vapour pressure, so they boil there first.

q3.text: Question 3. What happens to the bubbles when they reach the high-pressure part of the impeller?

q3-r0.text: A vent?! There's no tiny exit door inside the impeller.

q3-r1.text: Yes! They collapse, and the metal pays for it.

q3-r2.text: Quietly?! Ever heard a cavitating pump? It sounds like it's pumping gravel.

q3-r3.text: They don't even make it to the discharge. They pop on the vanes.

q3-b0.text: The bubbles are swept outward into higher pressure, and they collapse in an instant.

q3-b1.text: Each collapse fires a tiny jet of liquid at the metal. Thousands of them, every second.

q3-b2.text: That chips the vane. Like a tiny hammer, hitting it over and over.

q3-b3.text: The signs: a gravel-like noise, vibration, falling head, and a pitted impeller at overhaul.

q4.text: Question 4. Which change gives the pump more NPSH available?

q4-r0.text: Longer?! Every metre of suction pipe is a withdrawal from the account.

q4-r1.text: Hotter?! You just raised the vapour pressure. The bubbles say thank you.

q4-r2.text: Correct! More liquid above the pump, more NPSH.

q4-r3.text: A clogged strainer?! That's a toll booth on the suction line.

q4-ans.text: The answer: a higher liquid level in the tank.

q4-b0.text: Think of NPSH available as a savings account the liquid carries into the pump.

q4-b1.text: Deposits: the pressure on the liquid surface, and the liquid height above the pump.

q4-b2.text: Withdrawals: the vapour pressure, and the friction in the suction line.

q4-b3.text: If the balance beats what the pump needs, its NPSHr, plus a margin, no bubbles.

q4-b4.text: So: raise the level, keep the liquid cool, and keep the suction short, wide and clean.

q5.text: Question 5. A column bottoms pump handles liquid at its boiling point. What is its NPSH available?

q5-r0.text: Zero?! Then every reboiler pump in the world would be a gravel crusher.

q5-r1.text: Spot on. Height minus friction. That's all you get.

q5-r2.text: Same as a cold tank?! The liquid is literally boiling, my friend.

q5-r3.text: Half right. But the vapour pressure takes all of it back.

q5-ans.text: The answer: liquid height above the pump, minus friction.

q5-b0.text: At the boiling point, the vessel pressure and the vapour pressure are equal.

q5-b1.text: So the pressure deposit and the vapour pressure withdrawal cancel out.

q5-b2.text: Only the liquid height is left, minus the suction friction.

q5-b3.text: That's why bottoms pumps sit several metres below the column, with short, wide suction lines.

q6.text: Question 6. A pump starts crackling and its discharge pressure swings. What do you check first?

q6-r0.text: More speed?! The pump needs even more NPSH then. That's pouring petrol on it.

q6-r1.text: Throttling the suction?! That's squeezing the pump's straw. Never.

q6-r2.text: Yes! Check the suction side first. You'd make a great shift engineer.

q6-r3.text: Wide open?! More flow means more friction and a hungrier pump.

q6-ans.text: The answer: strainer, tank level and liquid temperature.

q6-b0.text: Start on the suction side. A dirty strainer, a low level or a hot liquid all drain the account.

q6-b1.text: Never throttle the suction valve. Control the flow on the discharge side.

q6-b2.text: If the pump runs far right on its curve, close the discharge a little. Less flow, less friction, and a lower NPSHr.

q6-b3.text: Then check the numbers with the NPSH calculator on pharmacheme dot in.
